initial_presentation: A 47-year-old female patient came to our clinic reporting reduced vision in her left eye.

A 3-year-old Saudi girl presented with a history of slowly growing, unruly scalp hair since early childhood. The patient has black hair that can be easily and painlessly pulled out with minor traction or combing. Her mother reported that the patient always had short hair and never needed a haircut. There is no consanguinity between the parents, and no similar condition is observed in her 3 older brothers, who have easily combable hair that requires regular haircuts. Clinical examination revealed no systemic abnormalities, with normal nails, teeth, and skin. There were no complete alopecic areas in zones subjected to rubbing or traction, but the hair pull test was positive.

A 64-year-old female presented with a painless, progressive swelling of the left lower extremity that had been ongoing for 1 year (Fig. A). The patient was obese, and her vital signs were within normal limits. She had no history of surgery or trauma affecting the inguinal or lower extremity lymphatic system. Additionally, she reported no allergies, no family history of similar conditions, and had never traveled overseas. Physical examination revealed that the left lower extremity below the inguinal line was significantly larger than the right side. Fibrotic changes and stemmer signs were noted on the affected side. There was no warmth or redness in the lower extremity. Measurements of leg circumferences taken 15 cm above the knee (AK) were 43 cm on the right and 52 cm on the left. Measurements taken 15 cm below the knee (BK) were 32.5 cm on the right and 36.5 cm on the left.

A 10-year-old girl presented with an 8-month history of skin changes on her right upper limb. The patient was in good health overall, with no notable family medical history and an unaffected twin sister. The skin changes initially appeared as bruise-like discolorations. On physical examination, there were atrophic, non-sclerotic, and band-like hyperpigmented plaques observed on her right forearm and upper arm.

A 23-year-old male patient presented to the hospital on October 11, 2020, with a primary complaint of a persistent cough lasting 4 months accompanied by fever. Previous antibiotic treatments had not been effective. The patient's medical history was otherwise unremarkable. Physical examination revealed signs of anemia and palpable lymph nodes in the bilateral submandibular and left axillary regions. The right submandibular lymph node measured 1.5 cm × 1.5 cm, while the left submandibular lymph node measured 4 cm × 4 cm. No enlargement of internal organs was noted.

The patient is a 52-year-old male with a history of chronic productive cough lasting 7 years, which began after relocating to a new office. The cough was more severe at night and aggravated by exposure to cigarette smoke. The sputum was white, sticky, and difficult to expectorate.

A 66-year-old woman with a history of post-traumatic epilepsy and hypothyroidism was brought to the emergency department following a seizure at home. She had been on phenytoin for over 40 years, but her husband noted inconsistent medication adherence and lack of recent neurologist visits. While watching television, she saw flashing lights, followed by generalized tonic stiffening with an atonic component, resulting in head trauma from hitting a table. This was followed by generalized clonic movements and urinary incontinence. The episode lasted 27 minutes and resolved without pharmacologic intervention. The patient had no memory of the event. In the emergency department, her phenytoin level was 6.3 mcg/mL (therapeutic range 10.0-20.0 mcg/mL).

A 28-year-old woman from Porto Alegre presented with widespread skin pigmentary changes and photosensitivity since childhood, along with skin and mucous membrane fragility. No similar cases were reported in her family. Physical examination of the skin showed significant atrophy on the back of the hands and feet, with a few scattered erosions and resolving blisters. There was extensive dyschromia on the limbs and trunk, and a loss of dermatoglyphics on her fingers. Oral examination revealed erosive stomatitis. The patient also reported inflammation in the esophagus, vagina, and anus, which led to stricture formation and required surgical correction.

In August 2019, a 22-year-old Chinese woman, born to consanguineous parents, experienced generalized tonic-clonic seizures (GTCS). Her early physical and intellectual development was typical, and there was no relevant family medical history.
